chapter_theme: Poykaiyar's battlefield of the Chola Senganan, the red-eyed wrathful Maal, lord of the Kaveri's watered land: each poem fixes one sight of the field in a simile, mostly of falling elephants (sinking mountains, snakes struck by thunder, a god's ploughing), with severed limbs, umbrellas and drums, the wailing kin, the taking of Kalumalam and the killing of the Vanji king, and each ends on the field where he killed his foes.

21.reading: Elephants with paired spears sunk in their chests and their wounds deepening, swaying under the arrows, with nothing to lean on and their old strength gone, stagger slowly like mountains whose footing the ground swallows, on the field where the red-eyed, wrathful Maal fought.
21.nuance: The mountain does not fall; the ground takes its foot (நிலம் கால் கவரும்), so the image is of slow subsidence, not collapse: the elephant goes down by degrees. செங்கண் சினமால், 'the red-eyed wrathful Maal', is the king's epithet that recurs through the book.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the wounded elephants sinking as they stagger

22.reading: Under umbrellas fallen to the ground, the trunks of the stately elephants with lined brows, cut through by the flashing swords of warriors who do not flee, lie across the umbrellas like a snake licking the bright crescent moon, on the field where the lord of the land of rushing water, with his thunderous drum, killed those who would not join him.
22.nuance: The white umbrella is the moon and the cut trunk the snake that swallows it at an eclipse, so the fallen umbrella, the sign of a king, is shown eclipsed. The snake rests on an emendation: the line prints நக்கும்பரம் பொக்குமே, read here as நக்கும் பாம்பு ஒக்குமே.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: a severed trunk lying over a fallen white umbrella

23.reading: Where the strong men hurled their spears up and split the foreheads, the elephants' bodies rising out of the stream of blood look like dark clouds in a red evening sky, on the field where Chempiyan, of the conquering spear army and the strong flagged chariots, killed his enemies.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the dark elephant bodies standing in the blood

24.reading: The fresh heads that strong-shouldered warriors struck off roll on the ground in every direction, much as fruit lies in a palmyra grove a great gale has passed through, on the field where the lord of the Kaveri's watered land, with his fragrant garland, killed those who would not come near.
24.nuance: The heads are not said to be like fruit; the grove after the gale is set beside them, and the reader supplies the fallen palmyra nuts. Our text has no comparison marker in line 3 (புக்கேற்ற); tamilvu's புக்கற்றே would supply one (அற்று, 'like').

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the severed heads rolling over the field

25.reading: Elephants that will not hold their ground charge like mountains that leap and set other mountains shaking, and as they charge the flags rise and surge as if to sweep the sky, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed those who did not love him.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the charging elephants
the flags rising over the charge

26.reading: A red-eared, dun male vulture rises with a hand that warriors running everywhere had cut off, and looks like the red-beaked Garuda climbing the sky with a five-hooded snake in its grip, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed his enemies.
26.nuance: The five fingers of the hand make the five hoods of the snake (ஐவாய்), so the grisliest sight of the field is turned into the god's bird carrying its prey; the simile works by exact count, not by mood.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.vehicle: ஐவாய் வயநாகங் கவ்வி விசும்பிவருஞ் செவ்வா யுவணத்திற்
comparisons.tenor: the vulture flying up with a severed hand

27.reading: Blood trodden out by elephants that stamp in rage as they wade through red mire gathers and stands in pools like great vessels of flower-water, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed those who did not love him.
27.nuance: The pools are the elephants' own footprints, filled; the vehicle is a festive thing, great jars of flower-scented water, so the field is made to look like preparations for a feast.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the pools of blood in the elephants' footprints

28.reading: In the press where warriors who do not flee, swelling with rage and fury, flash their glorious swords, a creature runs off with a great hand severed along with its shield and stuffs it in its mouth, and to the bewildered the sight looks like people gazing into a mirror, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed those who would not come near.
28.nuance: The shield held before the face by a dead hand makes the mirror; the poet says the likeness holds only for those whose sight is confused (மயலார்க்கு), a rare admission that the simile is a trick of the eye.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the beast holding the severed hand and its shield up to its face

29.reading: Like a flock of peacocks in a guarded grove that scatter each its own way when the wind strikes and a sudden crack startles them, those who have lost their kin cry out in all four directions on the field where the red-eyed, wrathful Maal fought.
29.nuance: This is the one poem of the chapter whose subject is the living: the enemy's kin (கேளிர் இழந்தார்), seen as birds startled out of a guarded grove, still sit inside a poem whose last line credits the field to the victor.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the bereaved kin scattering and wailing

30.reading: As a flood strikes and folds things over and rolls boulders down the hill, the bright blood pooled in the field drags along the killing elephants, on the field where the wrathful Maal of unbending valour killed those who would not submit.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the blood that drags the elephants

31.reading: Where warriors who do not flee hurled and split the brow, the fine plate on the frontal globe of the tusked killer elephant flashes like a streak of lightning, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed those who were not his friends.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's forehead plate flashing as it falls

32.reading: The good woman called Earth, of the fine body without a stain, has turned red as if she had wrapped herself in a red cloth, on the field where the lord of the battling watered land, whose drum is garlanded with flowers and never fails, killed those who raged against him.
32.nuance: The earth is made a woman who has dressed for an occasion, so the blood is a garment she chose; the line goes no further, and the gentleness of நல்லவள் against the matter is the point.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the earth soaked in blood
the earth of the battlefield

33.reading: Like vaalai fish leaping here and there among the water-lilies wherever the water rushes from a burst tank, the bright swords with their fine shining blades flash and spread, on the field where Chempiyan, of the horses with trimmed manes and the strong flagged chariots, killed his enemies.
33.nuance: The broken tank is a picture of plenty in the Kaveri land, so the poet borrows the Chola country's most domestic sight, fish in the field channels, for the swords.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the swords flashing through the ranks

34.reading: In the crowded clash, the young men who rose to meet the charge hurl their gleaming spears, and the small jackal tugging at the guts that slipped out and spilled looks like a hunting dog straining on its chain at a post, on the field where Chey of the heavy fresh ornaments fought and killed.
34.nuance: The entrail is the chain: the jackal pulls against what holds it as a leashed dog pulls against its tether. சேய் names the king as the red, Murugan-like one.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the jackal pulling at the spilled entrails

35.reading: As when a lion on the summit of a red mountain is broken by thunder together with that mountain, the famed lance plunged in and the enemy king fell with his royal elephant, on the field of the lord of the Kaveri land, whose river brims and comes down breaking its banks.
35.nuance: The lion is the king and the mountain his elephant, so the simile keeps their unity in the fall: neither goes down alone. This is the only poem of the chapter whose last line names a fallen king rather than the victor's killing.

thinai_evidence.note: the enemy king falls with his state elephant on the victor's field

comparisons.vehicle: செவ்வரைச் சென்னி யரிமானோ டவ்வரை ஒல்கி யுருமிற் குடைந்தற்றான்
comparisons.tenor: the enemy king and his elephant falling together

36.reading: Oh, the likeness matches without a flaw: on the day the lord of the Kaveri land took Kalumalam, the enemies' umbrellas, kicked by the horses, all turned upside down like mushrooms kicked over by cows, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed those who did not love him.
36.nuance: The poet praises his own simile before he gives it (உவமன் உறழ்வின்றி ஒத்ததே): horse for cow, umbrella for mushroom, the match is part for part. The umbrella, sign of a king's shelter, becomes a pasture weed.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names the day of the king's victory at Kalumalam

comparisons.tenor: the enemy umbrellas overturned by the horses

37.reading: The blood that the kings' corpses poured out, dragging with it the drums and the elephants with pearl-bearing tusks, looks in every direction like boats meeting on the sea, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed his enemies.
37.nuance: The drums, which spoke for the kings, float away on their blood; the pearls in the tusks make the sea of the simile literal at one point, since pearls come from the sea.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the drums and elephant carcasses floating on the blood

38.reading: Many elephants with harness on their thick necks, their wounds deepening, roll like snakes struck by thunder, on the field where Chempiyan, of mighty battle strength, the gold chain on his chest and the wrought anklet on his foot, killed those who would not come near.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the wounded elephants rolling on the ground

39.reading: In the confused clash where strength was bound to strength, the white umbrella, torn from its staff and gone, scoops up flesh and looks like a tray heaped with cotton, on the field where the lord of the watered land killed the king of Vanji.
39.nuance: This is the chapter's one poem that names the loser, வஞ்சிக்கோ, the Chera of Vanji. The umbrella that should shade a king now serves as a dish; line 1 (மைந்துகால் யாத்து) is obscure, and the reading of it here is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names the defeated Chera, the king of Vanji

comparisons.tenor: the overturned white umbrella holding flesh

40.reading: As though the god with the silver-white plough were ploughing the world, all the elephants went down to the ground, on the field where the red-eyed, wrathful Maal, with his army of many spears and roaring drums, poured down a rain of arrows.
40.nuance: Battle as ploughing is the old kalavazhi figure; here the ploughman is the white god with the plough, and the ploughshares are the falling elephants themselves, so the king's field is tilled on a cosmic scale.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's arrow-rain fells the enemy elephants

comparisons.tenor: the elephants falling and furrowing the field
the volleys of arrows

41.reading: Elephants pierced in the chest by the strong men's spears, unable to keep their footing, reel and lay their ears down as if listening to a secret the great earth is telling, on the field where the lord of the land of rushing water, with his thunderous drum, killed those who would not join him.
41.nuance: மறை can be the Veda or a secret; either way the fallen elephant's ear on the ground is turned into attention, the earth speaking and the dying listening. Lines 4 and 5 repeat the close of 22.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the field where the king killed his foes, the victory the kalavazhi celebrates

comparisons.tenor: the dying elephants lying with an ear to the ground

links.note: Kalavazhi 36 sings the day the Kaveri lord took Kalumalam (கழுமலங் கொண்டநாள்), the enemy umbrellas overturned like mushrooms; Akananuru 44, a hero hurrying home after his king's war, names the Chola Senni who took Kalumalam and captured Kanaiyan (கணையன் அகப்படக் கழுமலம் தந்த) and likens the heroine to that king's rich town Kudavayil.
links.teaches: Kalavazhi leaves the loser at Kalumalam unnamed and shows only the carnage, while the akam poet names the captive Kanaiyan and spends the victory as a mark of the Chola's prosperity, so together they show one battle remembered both as a field of dead and as a byword for a well-kept land.

links.note: Kalavazhi 39 ends on the field where the Chola killed the Vanji king (வஞ்சிக்கோ), his white umbrella torn down and full of flesh; Purananuru 74 is a Chera king's own poem from captivity, held like a chained dog (தொடர்ப்படு ஞமலியின்) and begging water. The two are tied by the tradition that the Chera defeated in Kalavazhi was Kanaikkal Irumporai, the poet of Purananuru 74; neither text in our corpus states it.
links.teaches: The victor's song counts the Chera's defeat as the end of the matter, but the defeated king's poem says that being taken alive and fed by strangers is worse than the sword, so on that reading the field the Kalavazhi praises produced a fate its own frame cannot see.

links.note: Purananuru 19 has the cut-trunked elephants rolling on the ground like ploughs (நாஞ்சில் ஒப்ப நிலமிசைப் புரள) in a field where old mothers weep for their sons; Kalavazhi 40 has all the elephants fall as if the god of the silver plough (வெள்ளிவெண் ணாஞ்சிலான்) were ploughing the world.
links.teaches: The Purananuru simile sits beside the mothers' grief, while the Kalavazhi lifts the same plough image to a god's tillage and drops the mourners, showing how the battlefield-as-ploughing figure grew into a frame of pure praise once the kalavazhi became a genre of its own.

links.note: Purananuru 25 praises Chezhiyan because his spear stopped short when he saw the enemy's widows beat their breasts and cut their hair; Kalavazhi 29 shows the enemy's bereaved kin wailing in all four directions and closes on the Chola's field.
links.teaches: Both poets put the defeated side's mourners in a victory poem, but one makes the king's restraint before them the glory and the other makes their wailing part of the spectacle of the field, so the pair shows two incompatible uses of the same grief in royal praise.

links.note: Purananuru 62 describes a field where both kings fell, the umbrellas shook, the famous drums were lost and no one was left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi 37 has the kings' corpses pour out blood that carries off the drums and the elephants, and the field belongs to the lord of the watered land.
links.teaches: The same lost drums and dead kings make a kalavazhi only because one king survives to own the field; Purananuru 62 shows the case where nobody does, and the poet must turn the praise to the heavenly guests, which marks the victor as the genre's precondition.

links.note: Kural 773 says fierceness is great manhood, but help given when misfortune befalls the foe is its cutting edge; Kalavazhi 35 ends with the enemy king falling with his royal elephant, struck like a lion on a thunder-struck mountain, and goes no further.
links.teaches: The Kural locates the height of valour in the moment after the foe falls, and the kalavazhi, built to stop at the field of killing, has no place for that moment, so the couplet names exactly what the battle-song leaves out.

links.note: Kural 774 praises the warrior who sends his spear off in an elephant and laughs as he plucks another from his own body; in Kalavazhi 23 the strong men (வயவர்) hurl and split the elephants' foreheads, and the field is Chempiyan's.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the spear-thrower's own pride and wound in view, while the battle-song shows the same feat only through the speared elephants and credits it to the king, so the pair shows the warrior's deed moving from his ethic into his lord's fame.

source_issues: 21-41: the core records carry no colophon thinai or thurai; every poem is marked vaakai here as a kalavazhi (the battlefield sung after victory), so puram_thurai is empty throughout.
22 line 4: நக்கும்பரம் பொக்குமே does not parse; read as நக்கும் பாம்பு ஒக்குமே (a snake licking the moon).
24 line 3: our text புக்கேற்ற has no comparison marker; tamilvu reads புக்கற்றே, which supplies one. Marked as juxtaposition and uncertain.
28: the creature that carries off the severed hand (இகலன், line 4) is not identified with confidence; Project Madurai's variant keys give ஓரி and other readings.
40 line 3: போர்த்தானைடச் carries a stray ட; read போர்த்தானைச்.
41: printed without a number and numbered 41 by its place; the site lacks it, and its lines 4-5 repeat 22 lines 5-6 (பாய்ப்புன / பாய்புன).
25 line 4 repeats 27 line 4 and 36 line 5 (புனனாடன் மேவாரை யட்ட களத்து), the book's refrain.
21 line 1 (மருமத்து), 27 line 3 (பூநீர் வியன்றமிடா), 30 line 3 (மடங்கா), 32 lines 1-2: the flags and variants show competing readings; the sense marked does not turn on them except at 27.
